processing: In the best-known version, Lushan Yunwu, young shoots are spread out, fixed, cooled, rolled, shaped into strips, tightened and dried. Other mist teas are made by their own local methods, usually as green tea.
harvest_season: As with most Chinese green teas, spring is the prized picking; exact dates depend on the mountain and its altitude.
appearance_dry: Lushan Yunwu is tight, sturdy green strips with plenty of fine white down; other mist teas vary.
appearance_liquor: Clear and bright, usually a pale yellow-green.
appearance_wet: As is typical of tender spring green tea, soft young shoots in a fresh green.
taste_profile: Lushan Yunwu has a fresh, lasting aroma and a mellow, slightly sweet taste. Teas from other mountains differ, so the name alone does not promise a flavour.

brewing.notes: Usual green tea practice: a glass or porcelain cup and water well off the boil. Pour the water in gently so the down does not make the liquor cloudy.

vintage_note: Sold like other Chinese greens, as the current spring harvest, and best drunk within about a year. Look for the mountain on the label: 'yun wu' alone is not an appellation, while Lushan Yunwu has been a protected geographical indication since 2004.
description:
Yun wu means clouds and mist, and the name describes where a tea grows more than a single recipe. It is attached to teas from misty mountains in several parts of China, and the famous one by far is Lushan Yunwu from Jiangxi.

On Lushan the main gardens sit above about 800 metres, around places such as Hanpokou and Wulaofeng, and the mountain is said to see mist on up to 195 days a year. Higher gardens are generally thought to give better aroma and taste.

The Lushan tea is made from young shoots of small- to medium-leaf plants, finished into tight green strips full of white down. In the cup it is clear and bright, with a lasting fresh aroma and a mellow sweetness. Treat it gently as you would any tender green: cooler water and no long stewing.

Other mist teas carry the name too, among them Yingshan Yunwu from Hubei. They are separate teas, so when you buy, the question to ask is which mountain and which spring.
history:
Lushan grew tea long before the name appeared: monks at its temples are credited with growing tea in the Eastern Jin and Southern dynasties, and production is described as rising in the Tang and peaking in the Song. The name Lushan Yunwu dates from the Ming dynasty.

In 1959 Lushan Yunwu was named one of China's ten famous teas, and in 2004 it became a protected geographical indication product. Little is documented about how the general term spread to teas from other mountains.
